Proposition 5: Statewide Officers
Proposition 5: Statewide Officers
Proposition 5: Changes Recall Election Process for Statewide Officers. Legislative Constitutional Amendment.
Additional Titles
Recall Reform, Eliminate State Officer Recall Successor Elections Amendment
Summary
The California Senate introduced Senate Constitutional Amendment 1 (SCA) in January of 2023. As the Legislature cannot amend the California Constitution by passing legislation, the amendment must be approved by California voters. The Senate passed the bill in February of 2024 and the Assembly passed an amended version in August of 2024. The Senate agreed with the changes to the bill sending the proposed constitutional amendment to voters on the November 2026 ballot as Proposition 5.
Proposition 5 would amend California’s constitution by changing the recall process. Specifically, it would eliminate the part of the ballot that asks voters to choose a replacement for the official being recalled. If an official is recalled, the office would instead be treated as vacant and filled under the existing state constitution and state law. Legislative vacancies would generally be filled through a separate special election, while most other statewide offices would be filled by appointment by the Governor. If the Governor is recalled, the Lieutenant Governor would take over, either temporarily until the next statewide election or for the remainder of the term, depending on when the recall occurs.
F iscal Impact
(Summary of Legislative Analyst's Estimate of Net State and Local Government Fiscal Impact)
The financial impact would depend on how often recalls occur and which offices are involved. Costs could increase by millions of dollars when a recall creates a vacancy that requires a separate special election, particularly for legislative offices. At the same time, eliminating replacement candidates from recall ballots could save millions in some elections by reducing ballot and election-material costs. Overall, Proposition 5 could result in either costs or savings of potentially millions of dollars per recall election, although the effect would be very small compared with the state’s overall budget.
What your vote means
YES: A “yes” vote supports changing California’s recall process so voters would decide only whether to remove an official, with the vacancy filled later under state law. A recalled official could run again, and the Lieutenant Governor would generally replace a recalled Governor.
NO: A “no” vote supports keeping the current recall process, in which voters decide whether to remove an official and simultaneously vote on who should replace that official if the recall succeeds.

Pro Con
Supporters argue that the current recall system can allow a replacement candidate to win with only a small share of the vote, particularly in low-turnout elections. They claim that Proposition 5 would make recalls more democratic and less confusing for voters while reducing opportunities to use recalls for political manipulation.
Opponents argue that voters should have the right to choose a Governor’s replacement at the time when they approve a recall. They say automatically allowing the Lieutenant Governor to take over could leave voters with a leader who shares the recalled Governor’s political views, limiting voter choice and weakening the purpose of the recall process.

California’s ‘orphaned’ ballot measures
By WILL MCCARTHY (https://www.politico.com/staff/will-mccarthy), JEREMY B. WHITE (https://www.politico.com/staff/jeremy-b-white) and NICOLE NORMAN (https://www.politico.com/staff/nicole-norman)
10/05/2026 03:09 PM EDT
State Sen. Josh Newman talks during a Senate session in Sacramento, California, on June 11, 2018. | Rich Pedroncelli/AP
LEFT BEHIND: Over the last two and a half years, California lawmakers spent countless hours drafting, debating and voting on a group of government reform ballot measures to put before voters. The same energy has not been put toward campaigns to pass them.
Proposition 5, which would change how successors are chosen in recalls, was set for the ballot way back in August 2024. Proposition 4, which would allow for the public financing of campaigns, landed in October 2025. Proposition 2, which would double the amount the state can deposit into its reserves, was rushed to the November ballot earlier this spring.
All aim to reform a somewhat wonky aspect of how government operates, and none of them are easily explainable to voters in a single sentence. And yet each of them have a limited, or non-existent public presence and campaign.
“You get these orphaned initiatives,” said Thad Kousser , a professor of political science at the University of San Diego. “So voters are left with very few bits of information on what’s going to be the most crowded ballot in a decade.”
The recall measure’s travails underscore how quickly a political window can close. In the aftermath of the failed attempt to recall Gov. Gavin Newsom , triumphant Democrats said they were determined to change a system that would allow a challenger — like MAGA tribune Larry Elder (https://www.politico.com/news/2021/08/17/ca-recall-election-larry-elder-505735) — to become governor with fewer votes than the number cast against a recall. Secretary of State Shirley Weber vowed action (https://www.politico.com/states/california/story/2021/09/15/california-elections-chief-wants-recall-overhaul-possibly-as-soon-as-2022-1391082), and election committees revved up (https://www.politico.com/newsletters/california-playbook/2021/09/16/with-newsom-secure-democrats-look-to-restrain-recall-494353).
But the momentum soon ebbed. Policymakers couldn’t agree on the changes. Polls showed voters were tepid on changing a process that many see as an important check on elected officials. By the time former State Sen. Josh Newman finally got his measure through, the Newsom recall — and the sense of urgency it engendered — were distant memories.
A spokesperson for the Prop 5 campaign did not reply to requests for comment, although Newman said in a recent interview that he was “not optimistic” about the recall reform measure’s chances.
Historically, the vast majority of measures placed on the ballot by the legislature have won — a full 69% between 1910 and 2025. In the past, that outcome has been largely a function of how many votes it takes for lawmakers to put measures before voters, a two-thirds majority of both houses traditionally meaning that the issue was highly popular.
But polling for the three government reform measures is scattershot. A September Public Policy Institute of California poll had Prop 4 and Prop 5 with only 42% and 35% support, respectively, while Prop 2 had the support of 60% of voters (a later Berkeley IGS poll put Prop 4’s support at 35% for, 35% against, and 30% undecided).
Prop 5 does not appear to have any financial backing or a campaign committee organized to pass the measure. The committee for Prop 4 has a single, $235,000 contribution from Movement Voter PAC, a progressive organizing group. Prop 2’s committee received a $150,000 contribution from Google last week.
Assemblymember Alex Lee , one of the coauthors of the legislation that placed Prop 4 on the ballot, said the measure was in a “good place” and that undecided voters are “ready to be persuaded.” The Prop 4 campaign has begun holding public events and is planning a bus tour at some point this fall.
“I knew the other marquee efforts would absorb the media attention,” Lee said. “Really it’s just about the voter education campaign.”
Assemblymember Jesse Gabriel , author of Prop 2, said you likely won’t see large ad spends or public appearances to drum up support for expanding the state’s budget reserves. Given the solid polling and what he called the “common sense wisdom” of the measure, he’s confident in its passage.
Meant to shield the state’s budget from the volatility of the stock market, the measure has the support of a wide range of groups, from the California Chamber of Commerce to SEIU. Even so, Gabriel said he expected a “lean campaign” that will “rely a lot on member-to-member communication.”
Each of the government reform measures share at least one key advantage: None face organized opposition.
“Its not like we have to raise X millions of dollars,” Lee said.
Welcome to Ballot Measure Weekly , a special Monday edition of Playbook PM focused on California’s lively realm of ballot measure campaigns. Questions? Concerns? Tips? TOP OF THE TICKET
A highly subjective ranking of the ballot measures — past and future, certain and possible — getting our attention this week.
1. Prop 37: The campaign for a measure to provide loans to help middle-income families purchase homes contributed $300,000 to the California Democratic Party last week, apparently viewing the measure in good financial standing.
2. Prop 38: The No on Prop 38 campaign is operating with a single six-figure check as it tries to run a campaign against billionaire Gary Michelson ’s immunology bond ballot measure. The $3,000 contribution comes from Robert Kaplan , the director of research at the Stanford School of Medicine Clinical Excellence Research Center. Michelson has contributed over $10 million to the initiative, which has come under criticism in recent weeks (https://www.sfchronicle.com/opinion/editorials/article/prop-38-money-california-22453646.php).
3. Prop 45: A group of Republican county organizations came out against Prop 45 last week, even as the Yes campaign faced scrutiny for donations (https://www.sacbee.com/news/politics-government/capitol-alert/article317427465.html) to Republican Assemblymember Carl DeMaio ’s Reform California organization (https://www.politico.com/news/magazine/2026/10/02/carl-demaio-california-maga-voter-id-prop-39-01103730). The Yes campaign, meanwhile, released a report (https://yesonprop45.com/report-2026-09-25-economic-and-fiscal-impacts-of-proposition-45/) showing what it says would be the “significant economic benefits” of Prop 45, including adding 20,000 homes a year.
4. Fund scientific research (2028): Newsom climbed the Golden Gate Bridge (https://x.com/CAgovernor/status/2105470383281598682) with State Sen. Scott Wiener and a camera crew to sign a $7.5 billion research bond that aims to combat federal funding cuts. The measure will be on the ballot in 2028. “I’m proud to sign a bond to invest in the future of the state of California,” Newsom said in a video from the bridge.
5. Prop 40: Heavily outspent and facing enormous establishment resistance, the wealth tax campaign is hoping America’s most prominent progressive can carry it to victory. Sen. Bernie Sanders is rallying for Prop 40 in Los Angeles today after swinging through San Francisco on Saturday, where he described the campaign as a Democrat-defining battle over “the most important ballot initiative in the country.” (https://www.politico.com/news/2026/10/03/bernie-sanders-billionaire-tax-san-francisco-rally-01105995)
6. Prop 39: DeMaio is continuing on his “Barbecue, Beer, & Ballots” tour through California, attending his tenth barbecue of the last week in Ramona (https://www.reformcalifornia.org/events/barbeque-beer-ballots-ramona-10-05-2026) today as the campaign looks to help pass Prop 39. As Will wrote for POLITICO Magazine last week (https://www.politico.com/news/magazine/2026/10/02/carl-demaio-california-maga-voter-id-prop-39-01103730?utm_source=firefox-newtab-en-us), DeMaio’s grassroots army has become a major factor in his rise in state politics.
7. Measure ER (Los Angeles County): A one-half cent sales tax narrowly approved by Los Angeles County voters in June took effect on Oct. 1. But it could be a while before the $1 billion it is expected to generate each year for health care can actually be spent. A lawsuit, brought by the Libertarian Party of LA County, will have to play out in LA County Superior Court before the proceeds can be used.
FIRST IN PLAYBOOK — Californians for Voting Rights, one of the committees organized to defeat Prop 39, is launching a pair of advertisements in the Bay Area hammering on the “consequences voters will face” should the measure pass. In the first spot, the No campaign characterizes Prop 39 as a “MAGA power grab” led by President Donald Trump (https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=cjk5YyP7FYM). The second warns people (https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=EbT1lgt8ic4) of longer lines in order to vote. The seven-figure buy is the committee’s first time on air.
IN OTHER NEWS
HE’S BACK: Former Gov. Jerry Brown will tonight join journalist Miriam Pawel , the author of nonfiction works about the Brown family (https://miriampawel.com/the-browns-of-california/) and Cesar Chavez (https://www.nytimes.com/2014/04/27/books/review/the-crusades-of-cesar-chavez-by-miriam-pawel.html), for a conversation launching her latest book: “California Dreams: The Making and Remaking of the University of California.” The discussion will “explore the history of the University of California, its relationship with California’s political and social life, and the continuing importance of public higher education,” and the event will run from 6 p.m. to 8 p.m. at the California State Library. The retired Brown’s appearance is his latest since he visited the state Capitol during end-of-session proceedings and penned a call for global nuclear (https://www.nybooks.com/articles/2026/10/08/i-taste-ashes-in-the-wind-nuclear-weapons-jerry-brown/) disarmament. Register here (https://libraryca.libcal.com/event/17654368) .
THE BOOGEYMAN: Democrats’ top Senate super PAC is flooding the airwaves with ads hitting Republicans on Jeffrey Epstein, the late financier and convicted sex offender. They have data to back it up, POLITICO’s Andrew Howard reports (https://www.politico.com/news/2026/10/05/democrats-smp-attack-ads-epstein-01106408).
Internal polling of over 4,500 voters from Senate Majority PAC, conducted by the Democratic firm Blue Rose Research late last week and shared with POLITICO, found that a 44% plurality of voters — including the same percentage of swing voters — think the Epstein issue is “serious” and that Republicans should be held responsible.
And while nothing trumps affordability as the issue du jour on the campaign trail this fall, state-level research from SMP found that the Epstein ads can shift races three to six points in Democrats’ direction.

***Recall of State Officials.*** The State Constitution allows voters to remove state officials from office before their term ends through a recall.
A recall is an election in which voters are asked whether to remove an official from office.
To qualify a recall for the ballot, supporters of the recall must collect a certain number of signatures from the official’s district (or statewide for statewide offices).

I'm noting that Berkeley IGS never polled Prop 5, since their guide only lists PPIC polls, and their September survey had Prop 43 at 31-40 instead. I'm also pulling a Politico base rate: legislature-placed measures have won about 69% of the time from 1910 to 2025.

Now I'm weighing a 69% historical pass rate for legislature-referred measures against the weak polling. The base rate may be inflated since those measures usually have broad support, and this one was a Democrats-only vote opposed by Republicans, which resembles earlier failed partisan measures like 2020's Prop 16. I'm also checking whether any poll covered Prop 5 directly, and the Emerson poll is still unclear on that.

I'm checking whether any poll besides PPIC covered Prop 5, and so far the only public one I've found is PPIC's. I'm also considering a Politico note that voters were tepid about changing the recall process. The 2024 Prop 5 is a close analog: a Democratic-only measure that polled 48-50 and then lost 45-55, so the yes share may erode from final polling.

I'm comparing the 2020 Prop 16 polling, which had the yes side in the mid-40s with undecideds, against its 42.3% result, and seeing the same pattern of yes support sliding after the final poll. That makes the 2024 analog and this one look alike, pointing toward a No outcome.

I'm checking the 2018 and 2022 California measures against the mid-40s yes pattern, and both fit: polls near 40-45 ended around 42-43. The 2024 PPIC poll had yes at 48 with 3% undecided, and it finished at about 45, so yes support slipped after the final poll. That makes a No outcome look more likely for this one.

I'm weighing whether the Prop 5 yes share might climb from September's 35 to around 48-50 by the final poll, which would undercut the No case. The shift could partly reflect a change in how the question was read, so I'm checking whether the wording difference explains it before giving that rise much weight.

I'm weighing whether a 2–5 point climb to Yes is plausible in the final two weeks without any campaign spending, since the typical pattern for these measures is a late slide rather than a late gain. I'm also considering that the 2026 environment looks strongly Democratic, so higher Democratic turnout could lift the Yes share somewhat more than usual.

I'm checking how a partisan turnout shift would move the yes share: Democrats at 56% yes, Republicans at 28%, independents at 40%. Under a hypothetical electorate of 45% Democrat, 25% Republican, and 30% independent, that comes to about 44%, so the answer depends heavily on how Democratic the final electorate turns out to be.

I'm checking the partisan math: even with Democrats at 56% yes, the blended share lands near 45%, so Yes would need an unusually Democratic electorate to reach 50%. The LA and Bay Area numbers near 50 don't carry the statewide total past it. Weighing that, I put Yes passing at roughly 20–30%, which points toward a No outcome.

I'm going to check for late news on Prop 5, including any new polls such as Emerson's and any endorsements, since nothing I've found so far changes the picture.

I'm going to search for an Emerson California poll from October on the propositions, a Los Angeles Times editorial on Prop 5, and any Newsom endorsement of it.

Endorsement: Prop 5 has a flaw so bizarre even its author doesn’t like it
Proposition 5 would overhaul California’s process for recalling state-level officials.
S.F. Chronicle from Getty Images elements
By Chronicle Editorial Board (https://www.sfchronicle.com/author/editorial-board/) , Opinion Staff Oct 8, 2026
So much has happened in American politics since 2021 that the recall election of California Gov. Gavin Newsom, which he overwhelmingly defeated, feels like a distant memory.
Proposition 5 (https://vig.cdn.sos.ca.gov/2026/general/pdf/prop5-text-proposed-laws.pdf) on the November ballot puts recalls back in the spotlight.
Endorsement guide: S.F. Chronicle Endorsements for the 2026 California Election (https://www.sfchronicle.com/projects/2026/california-sf-election-endorsements/)
Also: Y (https://www.sfchronicle.com/opinion/editorials/article/supreme-court-judge-california-22431608.php)es or no? Here are the Chronicle’s endorsements for California Supreme Court and appeals courts (https://www.sfchronicle.com/opinion/editorials/article/supreme-court-judge-california-22431608.php)
Authored by (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/billVotesClient.xhtml?bill_id=202320240SCA1) former Democratic state Sen. Josh Newman of Fullerton — who was recalled in 2018, won reelection in 2020 and lost again in 2024 — Prop 5 would overhaul California’s process for recalling state-level officials.
Advertisement
Article continues below this ad
Here’s how the current process works:
To recall a statewide official, proponents must gather signatures totaling at least 12% of votes (https://elections.cdn.sos.ca.gov/recalls/recall-procedures-guide.pdf) cast for that office in the prior election. For the Newsom recall, that threshold was 1.3 million signatures (https://admin.cdn.sos.ca.gov/elections/ccrov/2025/march/25024ra.pdf). To recall members of the state Assembly and Senate, the minimum number of signatures is 20% of votes (https://elections.cdn.sos.ca.gov/recalls/recall-procedures-guide.pdf) cast for that office in the last election — for Newman’s recall, that threshold was about 63,600 signatures (https://www.sos.ca.gov/administration/news-releases-and-advisories/2018-news-releases-and-advisories/recall-signatures-senate-district-29-certified).
Once a recall qualifies, voters then receive a ballot with two questions — one, should this official be recalled, and two, who should replace them? — and a list of replacement candidates. If a simple majority votes in favor of the recall, the replacement candidate who receives the most votes wins — even if that candidate only gets a fraction of the votes against the recall.
The two-question setup is confusing — only six other states use it (https://www.ncsl.org/elections-and-campaigns/recall-of-state-officials). And permitting someone to be elected without majority support is undemocratic. Furthermore, given the distraction and price of recalls — Newsom’s cost about $200 million during (https://apnews.com/article/elections-california-legislature-gavin-newsom-state-legislature-f8b78745cc5376dc4836d914352f2116) the most fraught moments of the pandemic — they should be reserved for cases of serious misconduct or abject unfitness, not petty grievances.
Advertisement
Article continues below this ad
Even though only 11 recalls of state-level officials have qualified for the ballot since 1913, according to the nonpartisan Legislative Analyst’s Office (https://lao.ca.gov/ballot/2026/prop5-110326.pdf), California could benefit from raising the bar. Its signature-gathering threshold is among the lowest in the nation (https://lhc.ca.gov/wp-content/uploads/Reports/266/Report266.pdf).
But Prop 5 doesn’t grapple with this issue.
Instead, it would eliminate the second question from the recall ballot, meaning voters would decide only whether the official should be removed.
If a majority says yes, one of three things would happen:
If the governor is recalled, the lieutenant governor would automatically step into the role. If the recall happens in the first half of a governor’s four-year term before the nomination period ends for the next statewide election, the lieutenant governor would serve until that election takes place and voters choose the next governor. But if the recall happens after that point, the lieutenant governor would finish the rest of the governor’s term.
Advertisement
Article continues below this ad
If another statewide official — such as the lieutenant governor, attorney general or secretary of state — is recalled, the governor would appoint their replacement. The governor already follows this process for statewide officials who die, resign or accept a different job.
And if a member of the state Legislature is recalled, the governor would call a special election for their replacement — mirroring the existing process for a lawmaker who dies, resigns or takes a different job. As the Legislative Analyst’s office notes (https://lao.ca.gov/ballot/2026/prop5-110326.pdf), if this special election couldn’t be consolidated with an already scheduled election, it could cost state and local election officials “millions of dollars” to administer.
Newman argued to us that eliminating the second question reduces “partisan games” and prevents candidates with minority support from winning elections.
We agree that the second question is problematic and we might support its removal in isolation. But Prop 5 contains a completely unnecessary provision that permits recalled officials to run in the very special election designed to replace them — overturning a ban in the California Constitution (https://law.justia.com/constitution/california/article-ii/section-15/).
This is particularly egregious because incumbents fighting recall attempts can generally raise unlimited funds from donors (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?sectionNum=85315.&lawCode=GOV). Although state law prohibits that money from being used for other campaigns, a recalled official in a special election is unlikely to forget whatever limitless support they received from wealthy special interests.
Advertisement
Article continues below this ad
Newman himself couldn’t explain why Prop 5 contains that provision.
“I’m honestly not sure,” he said. “It wouldn’t pain me if it wasn’t there.”

But it is there. And the inability or unwillingness of lawmakers to put forth a simple, clean reform effort is reason enough for voters to reject this measure.
California’s recall process can certainly be improved, but the problem isn’t so dire that voters need to accept Prop 5’s glaring flaw.

# Your guide to Proposition 5: Big changes to recall elections in California
...
Oct. 1, 2026 3 AM PT
...
Proposition 5 would change the way recall elections are conducted in the state by prioritizing voters’ right to oust an official before selecting a replacement.
The ballot measure also would make a major change to gubernatorial recall elections by automatically designating the lieutenant governor as the replacement.
...
### What will the measure do?
Under current law, when an elected official is recalled in California, the election for their replacement occurs at the same time.
This ballot measure would amend the state constitution to nix that system by first asking voters to choose whether or not to oust an official.
Then, in the event of a recall, the official would be replaced by appointment, succession or special election at a later date.
In that case, the former officeholder could run again.
The measure also would designate California’s lieutenant governor as the de facto replacement for a recalled governor until the next term.
### Who are the supporters?
Those in support include Secretary of State Shirley Weber, California Common Cause, the League of Women Voters of California and Lt. Gov.
Eleni Kounalakis.
### Who are the opponents?
Opponents include nonprofit Election Integrity Project California, Inc.

### What will the measure do?
Under current law, when an elected official is recalled in California, the election for their replacement occurs at the same time.
This ballot measure would amend the state constitution to nix that system by first asking voters to choose whether or not to oust an official.
Then, in the event of a recall, the official would be replaced by appointment, succession or special election at a later date.
In that case, the former officeholder could run again.
The measure also would designate California’s lieutenant governor as the de facto replacement for a recalled governor until the next term.
### Who are the supporters?
Those in support include Secretary of State Shirley Weber, California Common Cause, the League of Women Voters of California and Lt. Gov.
Eleni Kounalakis.
### Who are the opponents?
Opponents include nonprofit Election Integrity Project California, Inc.

Endorsement: Prop 5 has a flaw so bizarre even its author doesn’t like it
Proposition 5 would overhaul California’s process for recalling state-level officials.
S.F. Chronicle from Getty Images elements
By Chronicle Editorial Board (https://www.sfchronicle.com/author/editorial-board/) , Opinion Staff Oct 8, 2026
So much has happened in American politics since 2021 that the recall election of California Gov. Gavin Newsom, which he overwhelmingly defeated, feels like a distant memory.
Proposition 5 (https://vig.cdn.sos.ca.gov/2026/general/pdf/prop5-text-proposed-laws.pdf) on the November ballot puts recalls back in the spotlight.
Endorsement guide: S.F. Chronicle Endorsements for the 2026 California Election (https://www.sfchronicle.com/projects/2026/california-sf-election-endorsements/)
Also: Y (https://www.sfchronicle.com/opinion/editorials/article/supreme-court-judge-california-22431608.php)es or no? Here are the Chronicle’s endorsements for California Supreme Court and appeals courts (https://www.sfchronicle.com/opinion/editorials/article/supreme-court-judge-california-22431608.php)
Authored by (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/billVotesClient.xhtml?bill_id=202320240SCA1) former Democratic state Sen. Josh Newman of Fullerton — who was recalled in 2018, won reelection in 2020 and lost again in 2024 — Prop 5 would overhaul California’s process for recalling state-level officials.
Advertisement
Article continues below this ad
Here’s how the current process works:
To recall a statewide official, proponents must gather signatures totaling at least 12% of votes (https://elections.cdn.sos.ca.gov/recalls/recall-procedures-guide.pdf) cast for that office in the prior election. For the Newsom recall, that threshold was 1.3 million signatures (https://admin.cdn.sos.ca.gov/elections/ccrov/2025/march/25024ra.pdf). To recall members of the state Assembly and Senate, the minimum number of signatures is 20% of votes (https://elections.cdn.sos.ca.gov/recalls/recall-procedures-guide.pdf) cast for that office in the last election — for Newman’s recall, that threshold was about 63,600 signatures (https://www.sos.ca.gov/administration/news-releases-and-advisories/2018-news-releases-and-advisories/recall-signatures-senate-district-29-certified).
Once a recall qualifies, voters then receive a ballot with two questions — one, should this official be recalled, and two, who should replace them? — and a list of replacement candidates. If a simple majority votes in favor of the recall, the replacement candidate who receives the most votes wins — even if that candidate only gets a fraction of the votes against the recall.
The two-question setup is confusing — only six other states use it (https://www.ncsl.org/elections-and-campaigns/recall-of-state-officials). And permitting someone to be elected without majority support is undemocratic. Furthermore, given the distraction and price of recalls — Newsom’s cost about $200 million during (https://apnews.com/article/elections-california-legislature-gavin-newsom-state-legislature-f8b78745cc5376dc4836d914352f2116) the most fraught moments of the pandemic — they should be reserved for cases of serious misconduct or abject unfitness, not petty grievances.
Advertisement
Article continues below this ad
Even though only 11 recalls of state-level officials have qualified for the ballot since 1913, according to the nonpartisan Legislative Analyst’s Office (https://lao.ca.gov/ballot/2026/prop5-110326.pdf), California could benefit from raising the bar. Its signature-gathering threshold is among the lowest in the nation (https://lhc.ca.gov/wp-content/uploads/Reports/266/Report266.pdf).
But Prop 5 doesn’t grapple with this issue.
Instead, it would eliminate the second question from the recall ballot, meaning voters would decide only whether the official should be removed.
If a majority says yes, one of three things would happen:
If the governor is recalled, the lieutenant governor would automatically step into the role. If the recall happens in the first half of a governor’s four-year term before the nomination period ends for the next statewide election, the lieutenant governor would serve until that election takes place and voters choose the next governor. But if the recall happens after that point, the lieutenant governor would finish the rest of the governor’s term.
Advertisement
Article continues below this ad
If another statewide official — such as the lieutenant governor, attorney general or secretary of state — is recalled, the governor would appoint their replacement. The governor already follows this process for statewide officials who die, resign or accept a different job.
And if a member of the state Legislature is recalled, the governor would call a special election for their replacement — mirroring the existing process for a lawmaker who dies, resigns or takes a different job. As the Legislative Analyst’s office notes (https://lao.ca.gov/ballot/2026/prop5-110326.pdf), if this special election couldn’t be consolidated with an already scheduled election, it could cost state and local election officials “millions of dollars” to administer.
Newman argued to us that eliminating the second question reduces “partisan games” and prevents candidates with minority support from winning elections.
We agree that the second question is problematic and we might support its removal in isolation. But Prop 5 contains a completely unnecessary provision that permits recalled officials to run in the very special election designed to replace them — overturning a ban in the California Constitution (https://law.justia.com/constitution/california/article-ii/section-15/).
This is particularly egregious because incumbents fighting recall attempts can generally raise unlimited funds from donors (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?sectionNum=85315.&lawCode=GOV). Although state law prohibits that money from being used for other campaigns, a recalled official in a special election is unlikely to forget whatever limitless support they received from wealthy special interests.
Advertisement
Article continues below this ad
Newman himself couldn’t explain why Prop 5 contains that provision.
“I’m honestly not sure,” he said. “It wouldn’t pain me if it wasn’t there.”

But it is there. And the inability or unwillingness of lawmakers to put forth a simple, clean reform effort is reason enough for voters to reject this measure.
California’s recall process can certainly be improved, but the problem isn’t so dire that voters need to accept Prop 5’s glaring flaw.

But Prop 5 contains a completely unnecessary provision that permits recalled officials to run in the very special election designed to replace them — overturning a ban in the California Constitution (https://law.justia.com/constitution/california/article-ii/section-15/).
This is particularly egregious because incumbents fighting recall attempts can generally raise unlimited funds from donors (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?sectionNum=85315.&lawCode=GOV). Although state law prohibits that money from being used for other campaigns, a recalled official in a special election is unlikely to forget whatever limitless support they received from wealthy special interests.

“I’m honestly not sure,” he said. “It wouldn’t pain me if it wasn’t there.”

I'm noting that Berkeley IGS never polled Prop 5, since their guide only lists PPIC polls, and their September survey had Prop 43 at 31-40 instead. I'm also pulling a Politico base rate: legislature-placed measures have won about 69% of the time from 1910 to 2025.

Now I'm weighing a 69% historical pass rate for legislature-referred measures against the weak polling. The base rate may be inflated since those measures usually have broad support, and this one was a Democrats-only vote opposed by Republicans, which resembles earlier failed partisan measures like 2020's Prop 16. I'm also checking whether any poll covered Prop 5 directly, and the Emerson poll is still unclear on that.

I'm checking whether any poll besides PPIC covered Prop 5, and so far the only public one I've found is PPIC's. I'm also considering a Politico note that voters were tepid about changing the recall process. The 2024 Prop 5 is a close analog: a Democratic-only measure that polled 48-50 and then lost 45-55, so the yes share may erode from final polling.

I'm comparing the 2020 Prop 16 polling, which had the yes side in the mid-40s with undecideds, against its 42.3% result, and seeing the same pattern of yes support sliding after the final poll. That makes the 2024 analog and this one look alike, pointing toward a No outcome.

I'm checking the 2018 and 2022 California measures against the mid-40s yes pattern, and both fit: polls near 40-45 ended around 42-43. The 2024 PPIC poll had yes at 48 with 3% undecided, and it finished at about 45, so yes support slipped after the final poll. That makes a No outcome look more likely for this one.

I'm weighing whether the Prop 5 yes share might climb from September's 35 to around 48-50 by the final poll, which would undercut the No case. The shift could partly reflect a change in how the question was read, so I'm checking whether the wording difference explains it before giving that rise much weight.

I'm weighing whether a 2–5 point climb to Yes is plausible in the final two weeks without any campaign spending, since the typical pattern for these measures is a late slide rather than a late gain. I'm also considering that the 2026 environment looks strongly Democratic, so higher Democratic turnout could lift the Yes share somewhat more than usual.

I'm checking how a partisan turnout shift would move the yes share: Democrats at 56% yes, Republicans at 28%, independents at 40%. Under a hypothetical electorate of 45% Democrat, 25% Republican, and 30% independent, that comes to about 44%, so the answer depends heavily on how Democratic the final electorate turns out to be.

I'm checking the partisan math: even with Democrats at 56% yes, the blended share lands near 45%, so Yes would need an unusually Democratic electorate to reach 50%. The LA and Bay Area numbers near 50 don't carry the statewide total past it. Weighing that, I put Yes passing at roughly 20–30%, which points toward a No outcome.

I'm going to check for late news on Prop 5, including any new polls such as Emerson's and any endorsements, since nothing I've found so far changes the picture.

I'm going to search for an Emerson California poll from October on the propositions, a Los Angeles Times editorial on Prop 5, and any Newsom endorsement of it.

### What will the measure do?
Under current law, when an elected official is recalled in California, the election for their replacement occurs at the same time.
This ballot measure would amend the state constitution to nix that system by first asking voters to choose whether or not to oust an official.
Then, in the event of a recall, the official would be replaced by appointment, succession or special election at a later date.
In that case, the former officeholder could run again.
The measure also would designate California’s lieutenant governor as the de facto replacement for a recalled governor until the next term.

Endorsement: Prop 5 has a flaw so bizarre even its author doesn’t like it
Proposition 5 would overhaul California’s process for recalling state-level officials.
S.F. Chronicle from Getty Images elements
By Chronicle Editorial Board (https://www.sfchronicle.com/author/editorial-board/) , Opinion Staff Oct 8, 2026
So much has happened in American politics since 2021 that the recall election of California Gov. Gavin Newsom, which he overwhelmingly defeated, feels like a distant memory.
Proposition 5 (https://vig.cdn.sos.ca.gov/2026/general/pdf/prop5-text-proposed-laws.pdf) on the November ballot puts recalls back in the spotlight.
Endorsement guide: S.F. Chronicle Endorsements for the 2026 California Election (https://www.sfchronicle.com/projects/2026/california-sf-election-endorsements/)
Also: Y (https://www.sfchronicle.com/opinion/editorials/article/supreme-court-judge-california-22431608.php)es or no? Here are the Chronicle’s endorsements for California Supreme Court and appeals courts (https://www.sfchronicle.com/opinion/editorials/article/supreme-court-judge-california-22431608.php)
Authored by (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/billVotesClient.xhtml?bill_id=202320240SCA1) former Democratic state Sen. Josh Newman of Fullerton — who was recalled in 2018, won reelection in 2020 and lost again in 2024 — Prop 5 would overhaul California’s process for recalling state-level officials.
Advertisement
Article continues below this ad
Here’s how the current process works:
To recall a statewide official, proponents must gather signatures totaling at least 12% of votes (https://elections.cdn.sos.ca.gov/recalls/recall-procedures-guide.pdf) cast for that office in the prior election. For the Newsom recall, that threshold was 1.3 million signatures (https://admin.cdn.sos.ca.gov/elections/ccrov/2025/march/25024ra.pdf). To recall members of the state Assembly and Senate, the minimum number of signatures is 20% of votes (https://elections.cdn.sos.ca.gov/recalls/recall-procedures-guide.pdf) cast for that office in the last election — for Newman’s recall, that threshold was about 63,600 signatures (https://www.sos.ca.gov/administration/news-releases-and-advisories/2018-news-releases-and-advisories/recall-signatures-senate-district-29-certified).
Once a recall qualifies, voters then receive a ballot with two questions — one, should this official be recalled, and two, who should replace them? — and a list of replacement candidates. If a simple majority votes in favor of the recall, the replacement candidate who receives the most votes wins — even if that candidate only gets a fraction of the votes against the recall.
The two-question setup is confusing — only six other states use it (https://www.ncsl.org/elections-and-campaigns/recall-of-state-officials). And permitting someone to be elected without majority support is undemocratic. Furthermore, given the distraction and price of recalls — Newsom’s cost about $200 million during (https://apnews.com/article/elections-california-legislature-gavin-newsom-state-legislature-f8b78745cc5376dc4836d914352f2116) the most fraught moments of the pandemic — they should be reserved for cases of serious misconduct or abject unfitness, not petty grievances.
Advertisement
Article continues below this ad
Even though only 11 recalls of state-level officials have qualified for the ballot since 1913, according to the nonpartisan Legislative Analyst’s Office (https://lao.ca.gov/ballot/2026/prop5-110326.pdf), California could benefit from raising the bar. Its signature-gathering threshold is among the lowest in the nation (https://lhc.ca.gov/wp-content/uploads/Reports/266/Report266.pdf).
But Prop 5 doesn’t grapple with this issue.
Instead, it would eliminate the second question from the recall ballot, meaning voters would decide only whether the official should be removed.
If a majority says yes, one of three things would happen:
If the governor is recalled, the lieutenant governor would automatically step into the role. If the recall happens in the first half of a governor’s four-year term before the nomination period ends for the next statewide election, the lieutenant governor would serve until that election takes place and voters choose the next governor. But if the recall happens after that point, the lieutenant governor would finish the rest of the governor’s term.
Advertisement
Article continues below this ad
If another statewide official — such as the lieutenant governor, attorney general or secretary of state — is recalled, the governor would appoint their replacement. The governor already follows this process for statewide officials who die, resign or accept a different job.
And if a member of the state Legislature is recalled, the governor would call a special election for their replacement — mirroring the existing process for a lawmaker who dies, resigns or takes a different job. As the Legislative Analyst’s office notes (https://lao.ca.gov/ballot/2026/prop5-110326.pdf), if this special election couldn’t be consolidated with an already scheduled election, it could cost state and local election officials “millions of dollars” to administer.
Newman argued to us that eliminating the second question reduces “partisan games” and prevents candidates with minority support from winning elections.
We agree that the second question is problematic and we might support its removal in isolation. But Prop 5 contains a completely unnecessary provision that permits recalled officials to run in the very special election designed to replace them — overturning a ban in the California Constitution (https://law.justia.com/constitution/california/article-ii/section-15/).
This is particularly egregious because incumbents fighting recall attempts can generally raise unlimited funds from donors (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?sectionNum=85315.&lawCode=GOV). Although state law prohibits that money from being used for other campaigns, a recalled official in a special election is unlikely to forget whatever limitless support they received from wealthy special interests.
Advertisement
Article continues below this ad
Newman himself couldn’t explain why Prop 5 contains that provision.
“I’m honestly not sure,” he said. “It wouldn’t pain me if it wasn’t there.”

But it is there. And the inability or unwillingness of lawmakers to put forth a simple, clean reform effort is reason enough for voters to reject this measure.
California’s recall process can certainly be improved, but the problem isn’t so dire that voters need to accept Prop 5’s glaring flaw.

Opponents argue this initiative strips power from citizens and hands it directly to Sacramento political insiders

By Mercury News & East Bay Times Editorial Boards (https://www.mercurynews.com/author/mercury-news-east-bay-times-editorial-boards/)
PUBLISHED: November 2, 2026 at 4:32 PM PST | UPDATED: November 2, 2026 at 6:07 PM PST
Getting your Trinity Audio (https://trinityaudio.ai/) player ready...
Californians are being asked to vote “yes” or “no” on 14 ballot measures.
One of them is Proposition 5, which changes the recall process for statewide elected officials. According to the Legislative Analyst’s Office (https://lao.ca.gov/BallotAnalysis/Proposition?number=5&year=2026), the measure would remove from the question of who should replace the recalled official and proposes a special election to determine the replacement. In the meantime, the governor would choose who would fill the vacancy. In the case of a governor’s recall, the lieutenant governor would fill the vacancy until the next election.
Voting “yes” means the governor plays a much bigger role in replacing recalled officials and the lieutenant governor is a recall away from taking power (until the next election).
Voting “no” means the voters continue to choose replacements for recalled officials.
Supporters of the measure, also known as the Eliminate State Officer Recall Successor Elections Amendment, say this will simplify the recall process so we don’t end up with an overwhelming number of candidates on the ballot in a recall. With a greater number of candidates on the ballot, a candidate could win the election without a majority.
Opponents are uncomfortable with the increase in power given to the governor and insist it’s the people’s right to choose a governor’s replacement. They also say the lieutenant governor, with their proximity to the governor, would not represent the big change the people would have requested by voting for a recall.
In order to help you understand the pros and cons of the measure, we asked both sides of the proposal a series of questions.
Below are the answers from the No campaign, which have been edited only for length and clarity.
For the answers from the Yes campaign, go here (https://www.mercurynews.com/2026/11/02/we-asked-the-yes-on-prop-5-campaign-why-voters-should-approve-the-measure/).
What problem would Prop. 5 create?
A disincentive for the people to self-govern, leading to more distrust of government and restlessness of the “masses.” After a time of withdrawal and lack of participation, the people will feel and react to their oppression in a negative way. Oppressed people eventually revolt, and it’s never pretty.

We asked the Yes on Prop. 40 campaign why voters should approve the measure (https://www.mercurynews.com/2026/11/02/we-asked-the-yes-on-prop-40-campaign-why-voters-should-approve-the-measure/)

We asked the Yes on Prop. 41 campaign why voters should approve the measure (https://www.mercurynews.com/2026/11/02/we-asked-the-yes-on-prop-41-campaign-why-voters-should-approve-the-measure/)
We asked the Yes on Prop. 5 campaign why voters should approve the measure (https://www.mercurynews.com/2026/11/02/we-asked-the-yes-on-prop-5-campaign-why-voters-should-approve-the-measure/)
Currently, the recall process allows a candidate to win office without a majority. Why is that a system not worth reforming?
Under the current system, the democratic process of self-governance is served, and infinite amounts of taxpayer funds are saved by the current one-step process.
Prop. 5 “reforms” the current process by taking power from the people, and — worse — punishing the people for having the audacity to self-govern.
In the case of a recall, the term of office is limited to the remainder of the term of the recalled individual, and awarding the win to the person receiving a plurality in a crowded field is much more protective of the “democratic process” than adopting the changes proposed by Prop. 5, where the Sacramento insiders are the winners, hundreds of millions of dollars are wasted, and democracy dies.
If this measure isn’t a solution for fixing the recall process, do you have an alternate proposal?
This question pre-supposes the recall process needs fixing. The current process, wherein a recall decision and a filling of the recalled position in the case of recall success on the same ballot is efficient, fiscally responsible and respectful to the public.
The suggestion that the cost of having part two of the recall ballot is negligible, let alone millions of dollars, is patently absurd. Also absurd is the Prop. 5 proposal to eventually fill the recalled position with another, delayed election. The cost of a second election, which is likely to lead to a runoff costing more millions, is unarguable. That’s the very definition of absurd.
To quote Sen. Jones, “Our recall process is only ‘broke’ for those who find themselves on the business end of it, like Proposition 5’s author did when he (voted to raise) taxes after breaking campaign promises.”
What’s the biggest misconception about Prop. 5?
That there’s something wrong with the current system, and that CA legislators have any respect for a government of, by and for the people. CA is no longer a republic, but a socialist oligarchy. The power of the people to govern themselves has been so diminished already as to be virtually eliminated, and Prop. 5 is another step to seal the deal for complete power of the elite.
What did we miss? What didn’t we ask that our readers should know?
The element of Prop. 5 dealing with gubernatorial succession is also faulty. Yes, the people ostensibly elected a lieutenant governor, to serve as governor in the event of incapacity or death of the elected governor, not in the event of the governor’s disgrace — by which the lieutenant governor is surely tainted.
If the lieutenant governor wishes to succeed the governor in the event of a recall, that person may appear on the second portion of the ballot.
Chances are virtually 100% that if the people have grown disenchanted with the governor’s performance, they will be equally unwilling to be represented in that office by the second in command — almost certainly complicit in every act of disappointment and betrayal by the governor.

Californians are being asked to vote “yes” or “no” on 14 ballot measures.
One of them is Proposition 5, which changes the recall process for statewide elected officials. According to the Legislative Analyst’s Office (https://lao.ca.gov/BallotAnalysis/Proposition?number=5&year=2026), the measure would remove from the question of who should replace the recalled official and proposes a special election to determine the replacement. In the meantime, the governor would choose who would fill the vacancy. In the case of a governor’s recall, the lieutenant governor would fill the vacancy until the next election.
Voting “yes” means the governor plays a much bigger role in replacing recalled officials and the lieutenant governor is a recall away from taking power (until the next election).
Voting “no” means the voters continue to choose replacements for recalled officials.
Supporters of the measure, also known as the Eliminate State Officer Recall Successor Elections Amendment, say this will simplify the recall process so we don’t end up with an overwhelming number of candidates on the ballot in a recall. With a greater number of candidates on the ballot, a candidate could win the election without a majority.
Opponents are uncomfortable with the increase in power given to the governor and insist it’s the people’s right to choose a governor’s replacement. They also say the lieutenant governor, with their proximity to the governor, would not represent the big change the people would have requested by voting for a recall.
In order to help you understand the pros and cons of the measure, we asked both sides of the proposal a series of questions.
Below are the answers from the No campaign, which have been edited only for length and clarity.
For the answers from the Yes campaign, go here (https://www.mercurynews.com/2026/11/02/we-asked-the-yes-on-prop-5-campaign-why-voters-should-approve-the-measure/).
What problem would Prop. 5 create?
A disincentive for the people to self-govern, leading to more distrust of government and restlessness of the “masses.” After a time of withdrawal and lack of participation, the people will feel and react to their oppression in a negative way. Oppressed people eventually revolt, and it’s never pretty.

Currently, the recall process allows a candidate to win office without a majority. Why is that a system not worth reforming?
Under the current system, the democratic process of self-governance is served, and infinite amounts of taxpayer funds are saved by the current one-step process.
Prop. 5 “reforms” the current process by taking power from the people, and — worse — punishing the people for having the audacity to self-govern.
In the case of a recall, the term of office is limited to the remainder of the term of the recalled individual, and awarding the win to the person receiving a plurality in a crowded field is much more protective of the “democratic process” than adopting the changes proposed by Prop. 5, where the Sacramento insiders are the winners, hundreds of millions of dollars are wasted, and democracy dies.
If this measure isn’t a solution for fixing the recall process, do you have an alternate proposal?
This question pre-supposes the recall process needs fixing. The current process, wherein a recall decision and a filling of the recalled position in the case of recall success on the same ballot is efficient, fiscally responsible and respectful to the public.
The suggestion that the cost of having part two of the recall ballot is negligible, let alone millions of dollars, is patently absurd. Also absurd is the Prop. 5 proposal to eventually fill the recalled position with another, delayed election. The cost of a second election, which is likely to lead to a runoff costing more millions, is unarguable. That’s the very definition of absurd.
To quote Sen. Jones, “Our recall process is only ‘broke’ for those who find themselves on the business end of it, like Proposition 5’s author did when he (voted to raise) taxes after breaking campaign promises.”
What’s the biggest misconception about Prop. 5?
That there’s something wrong with the current system, and that CA legislators have any respect for a government of, by and for the people. CA is no longer a republic, but a socialist oligarchy. The power of the people to govern themselves has been so diminished already as to be virtually eliminated, and Prop. 5 is another step to seal the deal for complete power of the elite.
What did we miss? What didn’t we ask that our readers should know?
The element of Prop. 5 dealing with gubernatorial succession is also faulty. Yes, the people ostensibly elected a lieutenant governor, to serve as governor in the event of incapacity or death of the elected governor, not in the event of the governor’s disgrace — by which the lieutenant governor is surely tainted.
If the lieutenant governor wishes to succeed the governor in the event of a recall, that person may appear on the second portion of the ballot.
Chances are virtually 100% that if the people have grown disenchanted with the governor’s performance, they will be equally unwilling to be represented in that office by the second in command — almost certainly complicit in every act of disappointment and betrayal by the governor.

Currently, the recall process allows a candidate to win office without a majority. Why is that a system not worth reforming?
Under the current system, the democratic process of self-governance is served, and infinite amounts of taxpayer funds are saved by the current one-step process.
Prop. 5 “reforms” the current process by taking power from the people, and — worse — punishing the people for having the audacity to self-govern.
In the case of a recall, the term of office is limited to the remainder of the term of the recalled individual, and awarding the win to the person receiving a plurality in a crowded field is much more protective of the “democratic process” than adopting the changes proposed by Prop. 5, where the Sacramento insiders are the winners, hundreds of millions of dollars are wasted, and democracy dies.
If this measure isn’t a solution for fixing the recall process, do you have an alternate proposal?
This question pre-supposes the recall process needs fixing. The current process, wherein a recall decision and a filling of the recalled position in the case of recall success on the same ballot is efficient, fiscally responsible and respectful to the public.
The suggestion that the cost of having part two of the recall ballot is negligible, let alone millions of dollars, is patently absurd. Also absurd is the Prop. 5 proposal to eventually fill the recalled position with another, delayed election. The cost of a second election, which is likely to lead to a runoff costing more millions, is unarguable. That’s the very definition of absurd.
To quote Sen. Jones, “Our recall process is only ‘broke’ for those who find themselves on the business end of it, like Proposition 5’s author did when he (voted to raise) taxes after breaking campaign promises.”
What’s the biggest misconception about Prop. 5?
That there’s something wrong with the current system, and that CA legislators have any respect for a government of, by and for the people. CA is no longer a republic, but a socialist oligarchy. The power of the people to govern themselves has been so diminished already as to be virtually eliminated, and Prop. 5 is another step to seal the deal for complete power of the elite.
What did we miss? What didn’t we ask that our readers should know?
The element of Prop. 5 dealing with gubernatorial succession is also faulty. Yes, the people ostensibly elected a lieutenant governor, to serve as governor in the event of incapacity or death of the elected governor, not in the event of the governor’s disgrace — by which the lieutenant governor is surely tainted.
If the lieutenant governor wishes to succeed the governor in the event of a recall, that person may appear on the second portion of the ballot.
Chances are virtually 100% that if the people have grown disenchanted with the governor’s performance, they will be equally unwilling to be represented in that office by the second in command — almost certainly complicit in every act of disappointment and betrayal by the governor.

content.thinking:
I've confirmed from the electcademocrats.com page that Prop 5 has only PPIC polling, with IGS not testing it. Emerson's October poll may have covered only the governor's race, so I'm checking whether it included any ballot measures.

Emerson's poll looks like it only covered the governor's race and Newsom's approval, so it doesn't seem to include Prop 5. Next I'm going through the endorsements: the LA Times columnist's newsletter backs Prop 5, while the SF Chronicle and Mercury News both recommend voting no.

Next I'm going through the endorsements, and the reach of the No campaign is in question. The Mercury News piece on the No on Prop 5 campaign may show whether they have organized backing, so I'm checking that article.

I'm going to look at how Prop 5 has done in past California measures, starting with the 2024 analog where the final PPIC poll showed 48% yes against a 44.96% result. I'll check whether PPIC's September 2020 Prop 16 numbers follow the same pattern.

Checking the Wikipedia page for the 2020 Proposition 16 polling.

content.text: The electcademocrats poll summary also lists only PPIC for Prop 5. Next I'll check the Mercury News piece on the No campaign and the 2020 Prop 16 polling record as an analog for Democratic-backed amendments.

By Mercury News & East Bay Times Editorial Boards (https://www.mercurynews.com/author/mercury-news-east-bay-times-editorial-boards/)
PUBLISHED: November 2, 2026 at 4:32 PM PST | UPDATED: November 2, 2026 at 6:07 PM PST
Getting your Trinity Audio (https://trinityaudio.ai/) player ready...
Californians are being asked to vote “yes” or “no” on 14 ballot measures.
One of them is Proposition 5, which changes the recall process for statewide elected officials. According to the Legislative Analyst’s Office (https://lao.ca.gov/BallotAnalysis/Proposition?number=5&year=2026), the measure would remove from the question of who should replace the recalled official and proposes a special election to determine the replacement. In the meantime, the governor would choose who would fill the vacancy. In the case of a governor’s recall, the lieutenant governor would fill the vacancy until the next election.
Voting “yes” means the governor plays a much bigger role in replacing recalled officials and the lieutenant governor is a recall away from taking power (until the next election).
Voting “no” means the voters continue to choose replacements for recalled officials.
Supporters of the measure, also known as the Eliminate State Officer Recall Successor Elections Amendment, say this will simplify the recall process so we don’t end up with an overwhelming number of candidates on the ballot in a recall. With a greater number of candidates on the ballot, a candidate could win the election without a majority.
Opponents are uncomfortable with the increase in power given to the governor and insist it’s the people’s right to choose a governor’s replacement. They also say the lieutenant governor, with their proximity to the governor, would not represent the big change the people would have requested by voting for a recall.
In order to help you understand the pros and cons of the measure, we asked both sides of the proposal a series of questions.
Below are the answers from the No campaign, which have been edited only for length and clarity.
For the answers from the Yes campaign, go here (https://www.mercurynews.com/2026/11/02/we-asked-the-yes-on-prop-5-campaign-why-voters-should-approve-the-measure/).
What problem would Prop. 5 create?
A disincentive for the people to self-govern, leading to more distrust of government and restlessness of the “masses.” After a time of withdrawal and lack of participation, the people will feel and react to their oppression in a negative way. Oppressed people eventually revolt, and it’s never pretty.

We asked the Yes on Prop. 40 campaign why voters should approve the measure (https://www.mercurynews.com/2026/11/02/we-asked-the-yes-on-prop-40-campaign-why-voters-should-approve-the-measure/)

We asked the Yes on Prop. 41 campaign why voters should approve the measure (https://www.mercurynews.com/2026/11/02/we-asked-the-yes-on-prop-41-campaign-why-voters-should-approve-the-measure/)
We asked the Yes on Prop. 5 campaign why voters should approve the measure (https://www.mercurynews.com/2026/11/02/we-asked-the-yes-on-prop-5-campaign-why-voters-should-approve-the-measure/)
Currently, the recall process allows a candidate to win office without a majority. Why is that a system not worth reforming?
Under the current system, the democratic process of self-governance is served, and infinite amounts of taxpayer funds are saved by the current one-step process.
Prop. 5 “reforms” the current process by taking power from the people, and — worse — punishing the people for having the audacity to self-govern.
In the case of a recall, the term of office is limited to the remainder of the term of the recalled individual, and awarding the win to the person receiving a plurality in a crowded field is much more protective of the “democratic process” than adopting the changes proposed by Prop. 5, where the Sacramento insiders are the winners, hundreds of millions of dollars are wasted, and democracy dies.
If this measure isn’t a solution for fixing the recall process, do you have an alternate proposal?
This question pre-supposes the recall process needs fixing. The current process, wherein a recall decision and a filling of the recalled position in the case of recall success on the same ballot is efficient, fiscally responsible and respectful to the public.
The suggestion that the cost of having part two of the recall ballot is negligible, let alone millions of dollars, is patently absurd. Also absurd is the Prop. 5 proposal to eventually fill the recalled position with another, delayed election. The cost of a second election, which is likely to lead to a runoff costing more millions, is unarguable. That’s the very definition of absurd.
To quote Sen. Jones, “Our recall process is only ‘broke’ for those who find themselves on the business end of it, like Proposition 5’s author did when he (voted to raise) taxes after breaking campaign promises.”
What’s the biggest misconception about Prop. 5?
That there’s something wrong with the current system, and that CA legislators have any respect for a government of, by and for the people. CA is no longer a republic, but a socialist oligarchy. The power of the people to govern themselves has been so diminished already as to be virtually eliminated, and Prop. 5 is another step to seal the deal for complete power of the elite.
What did we miss? What didn’t we ask that our readers should know?
The element of Prop. 5 dealing with gubernatorial succession is also faulty. Yes, the people ostensibly elected a lieutenant governor, to serve as governor in the event of incapacity or death of the elected governor, not in the event of the governor’s disgrace — by which the lieutenant governor is surely tainted.
If the lieutenant governor wishes to succeed the governor in the event of a recall, that person may appear on the second portion of the ballot.
Chances are virtually 100% that if the people have grown disenchanted with the governor’s performance, they will be equally unwilling to be represented in that office by the second in command — almost certainly complicit in every act of disappointment and betrayal by the governor.

California voters decide 14 statewide propositions on November 3, 2026. On Kalshi and Polymarket, traders buy contracts on whether each one passes, and a contract’s price is the market’s chance. This page puts every measure side by side, with each venue’s price, and updates through the day.
For the separate statewide candidate contest on the same ballot, compare the California governor election (https://defirate.com/odds/california-governor/). For national races on the same election calendar, compare 2026 congressional midterm odds (https://defirate.com/odds/2026-midterms/); these proposition markets settle separate ballot questions.
How to read California proposition odds
A Yes contract pays $1 if the measure passes and nothing if it fails, so a price of 70¢ is a 70% chance. The average column is the mean of the venues that list the measure. Most proposition markets are thin: little money has traded, and the gap between the price to buy and the price to sell can be wide, so a single trade can move them. Prop 40, the billionaire tax, is the exception, with by far the most trading and its own markets on the margin of victory and on whether the tax takes effect.

How to read California proposition odds
A Yes contract pays $1 if the measure passes and nothing if it fails, so a price of 70¢ is a 70% chance. The average column is the mean of the venues that list the measure. Most proposition markets are thin: little money has traded, and the gap between the price to buy and the price to sell can be wide, so a single trade can move them. Prop 40, the billionaire tax, is the exception, with by far the most trading and its own markets on the margin of victory and on whether the tax takes effect.

PROP
5
CHANGES RECALL ELECTION PROCESS FOR STATEWIDE OFFICERS. LEGISLATIVE CONSTITUTIONAL AMENDMENT.
SUMMARY
Put on the Ballot by the Legislature
Under current law, voters elect replacement candidates at the same time as the recall election. This measure instead fills recall vacancies by subsequent special election or appointment. Fiscal Impact: Net fiscal effect unknown. In the event of a recall, savings or costs of millions of dollars to administer the election depending on the office recalled. Supporters: None submitted Opponents: None submitted
WHAT YOUR VOTE MEANS
YES
A YES vote on this measure means: Recall elections would no longer include a question about who should fill the vacancy. Instead, vacancies typically would be filled through special elections or appointments, depending on the office and timing.
NO
A NO vote on this measure means: Voters would continue to be asked who should fill the vacancy as part of recall elections.
ARGUMENTS
PRO
Proposition 5 restores the recall to its original purpose: removing corrupt officials. It closes the loophole that allows replacements to win with a small fraction of the vote, reducing the politics and costs of future recalls. Endorsed by League of Women Voters of California and California Common Cause. Vote YES
CON
Proposition 5 degrades California’s century-old recall process by limiting voters’ right to select a replacement for recalled officials. Instead, when statewide elected officials are recalled, other politicians would choose a replacement. For lower offices, another costly, taxpayer-funded election would come months later, leaving the office vacant and the people unrepresented.

Polling points to No, with PPIC showing 45 yes to 52 no in October and 35 to 59 in September, plus a forecast of about 45.7% chance of passing. So I'm leaning toward answering "no."

Whether the answer is "no" holds under either reading, since No is favored. Still, the post-election results pages might already be out, so I'll open the CalMatters and KCRA result trackers to check.

The contest looked to be a toss-up going into Election Day, with the no side holding a small edge. Welcome to CalMatters, the only nonprofit newsroom devoted solely to covering issues that affect all Californians. Sign up for WhatMatters (https://calmatters.org/subscribe-to-calmatters/whatmatters) to receive the latest news and commentary on the most important issues in the Golden State. California voters are weighing in on whether to change the state recall process that allows voters to remove elected officials from office before the end of their terms. Proposition 5 (https://calmatters.org/california-voter-guide-2026/proposition-5-recall-reform/) would break the recall process into two parts: Voters would first decide in an election whether an official should be removed from office. If successful, they’d vote again in a follow-up election on who should replace the recalled official. Under the current system, voters are asked both questions at the same time. Democratic lawmakers placed the constitutional amendment on the ballot in 2024. It was endorsed (https://www.abc10.com/article/news/politics/gov-newsom-announces-position-on-statewide-ballot-propositions/103-a92674ac-c53f-46cf-a625-6e469a288eed) by Gov. Gavin Newsom, who survived his own attempted recall in 2021. The outcome of Prop. 5 was far from certain going into Election Day: 45% of people polled in mid-October by the Public Policy Institute of California said they would vote for it (https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-their-government-october-2026/#:~:text=Bay%20Area%20(51%25).-,Proposition%205,-(Changes%20Recall%20Election), while 52% said they wouldn’t. The numbers were more even than voters’ response at first blush — a similar poll in early September (https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-their-government-september-2026/#:~:text=Proposition%205%20(Changes%20Recall%20Election%20Process%20for%20Statewide%20Officers).) found 59% of likely voters said they likely would vote no and just 35% said they would vote yes. Where Prop. 5 came from In the aftermath of the failed recall of Newsom in 2021, Democratic lawmakers and Secretary of State Shirley Weber began advocating for changes to the process. The Newsom recall effort cost taxpayers about $200 million, and another $100 was spent in the campaign to stop the recall by Newsom’s potential replacements to get their message out to voters. Newsom walked away unscathed, with 62% of voters electing to keep him in office. Weber and good governance groups argued (https://calmatters.digitaldemocracy.org/hearings/258090?t=338&f=d2d732fccac5f698c6d6489536c70cb8) the current system leads to unnecessary state expense, confuses voters, and can lead to ‘undemocratic’ outcomes, since the winner needs a plurality of the vote, not the majority, to win. They supported Senate Constitutional Amendment 1 (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/billNavClient.xhtml?bill_id=202320240SCA1), authored by Democratic Sen. Josh Newman, who was recalled himself in 2018. The effort became Prop. 5 when Democratic lawmakers passed it in 2024. Republican lawmakers voted against it, arguing (https://calmatters.digitaldemocracy.org/hearings/257408?t=362&f=816848bd63bbdd2078deeadec3321c8c) the reform was not needed, would dilute the power of voters and lead to additional special election costs because of the need to hold two elections. Unlike some of the tax measures on the ballot that have spurred multimillion-dollar spending sprees, no group has spent any money on the effort, according to CalMatters campaign finance tracker. Although recalls are often initiated, they rarely make it to voters (https://www.sos.ca.gov/elections/recalls/recall-history-california-1913-present). Only 11 recalls have made it to the ballot in California since 1913, and only six have been approved by voters. The current recall process is how Republican Gov. Arnold Schwarzenegger came into power, replacing Gray Davis in 2003. READ NEXT Democrats want to change the rules for recall elections.
